analysis.one_liner: Exempts private equity fund managers from SEC registration and reporting requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill exempting private equity fund advisers from SEC registration passed the House on March 22, 2012, but the Senate never voted on it, so it died.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2010 financial reform law (Dodd-Frank) required investment advisers to private equity funds to register with the SEC and open their books to examination. This bill would have undone that for private equity: it created an exemption from adviser registration and reporting, as long as a fund had not borrowed more than twice its invested capital, while directing the SEC to write rules requiring exempt advisers to keep records and file reports [S3] [S4]. It cleared the House Financial Services Committee in July 2011 [S6] and passed the full House on March 22, 2012, but the Senate never took it up, so it died at the end of the 112th Congress [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Private equity fund advisers and the funds they manage gain the most: they are relieved of SEC registration costs and regular SEC examinations. The bill's sponsors argued this would lower costs for small investment firms and, indirectly, the small businesses private equity invests in. Public pension funds and other large investors in these funds do not gain protection from the bill; its substantive protections for investors are limited to SEC recordkeeping rules.

how_it_helps.text: It repealed the 2010 requirement that private equity fund advisers register with the SEC, sparing those advisers the compliance costs of registration and reporting.

Its stated case was that the registration burden fell mainly on advisers who also manage small funds, raising costs for small funds without protecting investors, who in private equity are typically large institutions and wealthy individuals.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on the financial system's stability and transparency pay if fraud or excessive leverage inside lightly reported private equity funds goes undetected, as the public learned when lightly regulated funds concealed losses before 2008. The general public also loses visibility into a sector whose investment decisions can hollow out companies.

drawbacks.text: It removed the 2010 requirement that private equity fund advisers register with the SEC, ending regular SEC examination of how these funds manage pooled money.

The only real limit was a leverage cap — funds could still borrow up to twice their invested capital — but the bill let them skip the registration and reporting designed to catch excessive risk-taking before it hurts investors.
The exemption applied to advice about private equity funds regardless of fund size; critics argued it re-created the regulatory blind spot that helped conceal large Ponzi schemes before 2008.
It was pitched as helping small businesses and saving jobs, but nothing in the bill required funds to lend to or invest in small businesses — the benefits to them were indirect at best.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefits are secondhand and unproven: cheaper compliance costs for fund managers might trickle down to small companies or investors, but the public gain is speculative. The cost is real: the public loses the transparency it was given in 2010, when SEC-registered private equity funds were among the few corners of finance the public could examine after the crisis. The naming — "Small Business Capital Access and Job Preservation" — promised small-business and job benefits the bill did not directly deliver; its direct effect was a carve-out for a concentrated financial sector.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in March 2012, but the Senate, then run by Democrats, never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in March 2011 and cleared the House Financial Services Committee by July, reported with an amendment that added a leverage cap for the exemption.
The House passed H.R. 1082 by voice vote on March 22, 2012.
The Senate never voted on the bill or a companion, and it expired at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity advisers kept their SEC registration and examination obligations instead of winning a broad exemption, and the SEC kept visibility into how private funds manage investor money. Ordinary investors retained the post-crisis transparency rules rather than losing them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The SEC and private equity's regulators

sides.party_line_note: House Republicans led the bill, and only two of its ten cosponsors were Democrats; the House passed it by voice vote, while the Democratic-controlled Senate never acted on it.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and their advisers
industries.note: The bill would have repealed the registration requirement private equity advisers won under the 2010 financial overhaul, saving them compliance costs and keeping their books out of routine SEC examination. It carved out their regulator's oversight of them.

It stripped the SEC of the authority to register and examine private equity fund advisers, leaving only recordkeeping rules instead of full oversight. Regulators lose the visibility they need to catch fraud early.

industries.industry: Pension funds, endowments, and other institutional investors
industries.note: These are the main investors in private equity funds. Exempted advisers face lighter oversight of the funds they rely on, though the funds' institutional investors are sophisticated parties, not ordinary households.
